strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: unreliable minority-class predictions in imbalanced node classification. Expanding supervision through existing unlabeled nodes avoids synthesizing node features and graph connections and works with several GNN architectures.

The experimental coverage is substantial: five datasets, three GNN architectures, imbalance ratios up to 100, and five repetitions with reported uncertainty. Many gains are meaningful; for example, Cora/GCN at imbalance ratio 20 achieves 77.02% balanced accuracy versus 67.30% for the strongest reported baseline.

The pseudo-label accuracy analyses, ranking ablations, and sensitivity experiments provide useful evidence about when self-training succeeds or fails. Including naturally imbalanced Flickr and Computers-Random strengthens the evaluation beyond artificially reduced training labels.

The appendix documents dataset statistics, optimization schedules, hyperparameter search ranges, and hardware, providing a useful foundation for reproduction. The public-benchmark experiments raise no evident material research ethics concern.
weaknesses: The contribution beyond the closest prior work is insufficiently established. M3S, acknowledged in Section 6, already uses agreement between clustering assignments and classifier predictions to filter pseudo-labels, substantially overlapping with DPAM. The DPAM-plus-confidence ablations partially address this comparison, but equivalence to tuned M3S and matched training/selection budgets are not established. Comparisons with M3S and simple fixed-weight rank fusion are particularly important for assessing originality.

Core algorithmic definitions need clarification. Equation (7) adds sorted node lists without explicitly defining node-aligned rank vectors. Section 4.3 also identifies a node's assigned class with its nearest class centroid, although assigning an entire cluster through Equation (4) does not guarantee this for each member. These ambiguities affect the implementation and interpretation of the geometric filtering mechanism.

Supporting tables contain inconsistencies that materially weaken confidence in the diagnostic evidence. Table 8, GCN at ratio 5, reports 11,593.6 aligned plus 2,308.4 rejected nodes despite only 13,632 unlabeled nodes. Table 9 reports 96.40 ± 4.27 as mean accuracy ± standard error over five repetitions; for five accuracies bounded by 100% with that mean, the standard error cannot exceed 3.60. Corrected tables and clarification of the uncertainty calculation are needed.

Several conclusions overstate the results. On Computers-Random with GraphSAGE, UNREAL obtains 71.86% F1 versus 73.59% for GraphENS+TAM, contradicting the claim of consistent superiority on naturally imbalanced datasets. Table 11 also shows that DGIN sometimes reduces F1 and that some component gains are small relative to uncertainty. The paper should distinguish substantial improvements from inconclusive differences and failures.

Computational advantages are not adequately quantified. Appendix D specifies 40–100 training rounds, with up to 2,000 epochs per subsequent round, but provides no total runtime or measured peak-memory comparison. Baseline out-of-memory results on one GPU establish a practical limitation of those implementations, but do not establish overall efficiency. Comparisons with self-training under matched compute and tuning budgets are missing.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive appendix: selected configurations, the F1 averaging convention, weight reinitialization between rounds, and precise class-wise selection quotas are insufficiently specified. Furthermore, the across-ratio analysis changes training splits and majority-label counts while retaining one minority label at ratios 20, 50, and 100, limiting attribution of the observed trends specifically to imbalance.
